30 Dec 1970. Last log of the year. Board circular: decommission scheduled 1971. Twenty-two
years of nights. I will keep it well until they take it, and after, for nothing, because
a dark light still wants a keeper or it falls.
09 Feb 1971. Ice on the ninety-nine steps. Salted them. Nan did not come up. She has
stopped coming up.
21 Mar 1971. Roe's father died. Roe skippers the Marigold outright now, and worse for it,
being young and needing the money and afraid of neither weather nor me.
07 Jul 1971. Told Roe plainly the Marigold's lamp was untrustworthy and the bar unkind on
a spring ebb. He thanked me and did nothing. A warning given is a warning kept, whatever
follows. I have that, at least.
30 Oct 1971. Two weeks left of the working light. Nan's case is packed and stands in the
hall like a guest who will not sit. Wind SW 6.

EXAMINATION of Mr S. VANE, keeper.
Q. Mr Vane, was the Saltford light burning on the night of 14 November 1971?
A. It was my duty to keep it burning.
Q. That is not what I asked. Was it burning?
A. A light is kept, sir, or it is not. I kept it as I kept it every night for twenty-two
years.
Q. Did you at any time that night observe the Marigold in distress?
A. I observed weather no boat should have been out in.

A. There was nothing at the harbour I could have done that the sea had not already decided.

[DOCUMENT — Transcript — Saltford Light keeper's log, selected entries 1949–1968]
The early books, larger-handed, the ink browner. Selected entries only; the working
record of a keeper's life. Times in 24-hour form as kept.

02 May 1949. First night as keeper of Saltford. Old Pengelly handed me the log and the
keys and said mind the ninety-nine and mind yourself and went down them for the last
time. Wind SW 2. Light lit at 20:14. I did not sleep for watching it.
14 Sep 1949. Learned the lamp's every sound. It speaks if you listen. A keeper who cannot
hear his light by ear is no keeper.
06 Feb 1951. Married Nan Trewin at St Just. Brought her to the cottage in the rain. She
stood in the covered walk and looked up the ninety-nine steps and said, "You'll not get
me up there," and mostly I did not.
19 Nov 1953. Worst gale in memory. Force 10. Held the lamp through it, thirty hours
without the bed. Two ships stood off by my light and lived. That is the whole of the job
in one night.
30 Apr 1955. Edith born, at Truro, in the morning. I lit the lamp that evening as always.
A man does not stop the world for joy; he keeps the light, and the joy keeps beside it.
11 Aug 1958. Taught Edith the ninety-nine steps, counting each. She is three and counts
to ninety-nine before she can say her own name plain. Nan says I am making her strange. I
am making her careful, which is a kinder word for the same thing.
07 Jul 1959. Converted to electric. The paraffin days done. Cleaner, colder. I do not say
I miss the smell of the old light but I note that I have written this line.
23 Dec 1962. Ice storm. The gallery a chandelier. Edith seven, up the steps against her
mother's word, to see it. We stood and said nothing and it was the best hour of that year.
14 Mar 1965. Branch railway closed. The village a little more alone. The sea does not
notice our timetables.
30 Oct 1968. Twenty years next spring. The Board's letters come oftener now, and warmer,
which in the Board's tongue means the end is near. A warm letter from the Board is a cold
thing to a keeper.

[WORLD FACTS]
- Saltford harbour dries at low spring tide; boats sit on the mud. The bar is dangerous two hours either side of low water.
- The village lived on pilchard and crab; the fleet was six boats in 1971 and is two now.
- The Bethel chapel above the harbour closed in 1984. Its bell was sold to a farm at Zennor.
- Saltford's lamp was a first-order fixed catadioptric, paraffin-vapour until 1959, then electric. Its character was a fixed white light, not a flash.
- The branch railway to Saltford closed in 1965. The old station is a chandlery now.
- Saltford takes its name from the medieval salt pans east of the point, long since silted.
